solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

entries.clue: Output of sewer covers wide area with wee mostly (7,6)

indicators.note: most of the word, not all: the last letter goes

blocks.note: to blanket something is to cover all of a wide area
TITCHY = wee, small; 'mostly' drops the Y

annotation.surface: A grim report on what a sewage pipe spreads over the land.
annotation.walkthrough: The sewer is not a drain but someone who sews. TITCHY is British slang for very small.
annotation.definitionFit: Blanket stitch is an edging stitch, something a person sewing produces.

entries.clue: Champions scoff over club being a nuisance along the way? (4-4,6)

indicators.note: in a down clue, 'over' puts one piece above, so before, the next

blocks.note: to back someone is to champion them
scoff = eat greedily
a driver is a golf club

annotation.surface: Sports champions stuffing themselves before a club event and making pests of themselves on the road.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Champions' is a verb here, not a noun: it gives BACKS. The question mark flags the playful definition: the nuisance is on a car journey.
annotation.definitionFit: A back-seat driver is a passenger who pesters the driver with advice during the journey.

entries.clue: Penny in currency raised for end of tax year? (5)

indicators.note: the penny goes inside the currency
in a down clue, raised means written bottom to top

blocks.note: p = penny
the lira, former Italian currency; reversed it is ARIL, and P goes in after the A

annotation.surface: A penny tucked into a currency that has gone up just in time for tax year-end.
annotation.walkthrough: The UK tax year ends on 5 April, hence the question mark: April is only where it ends, not the end itself.
annotation.definitionFit: The British tax year runs to 5 April, so it ends in April.

entries.clue: Bane of comic character’s shtick ultimately: pity not funny in vacuous routine (10)

indicators.note: ultimately means in the end, so only the word's final letter is used
the letters are rearranged in a comic way
the anagram goes inside the emptied routine
empty: only the outer letters remain

blocks.note: last letter of shtick
ROUTINE emptied to its outer letters, holding the anagram
PITY + NOT rearranged, sitting inside R…E

annotation.surface: A critic's verdict that a comedian's shtick fell flat: pitiful, humourless, an empty routine.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Comic character' means a comic-book hero, Superman, not a funny person, though the surface pulls hard towards stand-up.
annotation.definitionFit: Kryptonite is the one substance that weakens Superman, the comic-book character.

entries.clue: Good man feeding animal a Mexican dish (7)

indicators.note: the good man goes into the animal, as food goes into a mouth

blocks.note: the toad, holding ST
a saint, ST, is a good man
taken as it stands

annotation.surface: A kind man handing an animal a plate of Mexican food.
annotation.walkthrough: 'A' belongs to the wordplay, not the definition, even though 'a Mexican dish' reads as one phrase.
annotation.definitionFit: A tostada is a fried tortilla with toppings, a Mexican dish.

entries.clue: Chest bone perfectly aligned, then pull leg? (4,3)

indicators.note: one piece follows the other

blocks.note: a true wall or wheel is perfectly aligned
to rib someone is to tease them, pull their leg

annotation.surface: A chiropractor straightening a chest bone and then yanking a leg.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Pull leg' sounds like physiotherapy but is the idiom for teasing.
annotation.definitionFit: A true rib is one of the upper seven pairs joined directly to the breastbone.

entries.clue: Asian moor on the phone? (4)

indicators.note: heard, not seen: a phone carries only sound

blocks.note: to moor a boat is to tie it up

annotation.surface: Someone asking whether an Asian caller is a Moor.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Moor' looks like a noun for a person or a heath; it is the verb for tying up a boat.
annotation.definitionFit: Thai means from Thailand, an Asian country.

entries.clue: Masses of chicken in Benidorm gobbled by two beneath house (3,6)

indicators.note: the chicken is swallowed by the two
in a down clue, these letters come under HO

blocks.note: HO is the abbreviation for house
two in Roman numerals, split around the chicken
pollo is Spanish for chicken; Benidorm is a Spanish resort

annotation.surface: Crowds of holidaymakers wolfing chicken at a Spanish resort.
annotation.walkthrough: Benidorm is a Costa Blanca resort popular with British package tourists, which makes the masses in the surface feel at home.
annotation.definitionFit: Borrowed Greek for 'the many', used in English for ordinary people as a mass.

entries.clue: Arcade looking lively in Cologne, residence empty (8,6)

indicators.note: the lively word goes inside the cologne
only the outer letters remain

blocks.note: cologne is a scent; it goes around HOPPING after its S
hopping about = lively
outer letters of residence

annotation.surface: A busy shopping arcade in the German city of Cologne, with one house standing vacant.
annotation.walkthrough: Cologne with a capital C looks like the German city; it is eau de cologne, a scent.
annotation.definitionFit: An arcade is a covered row of shops, a shopping centre.

entries.clue: Despicable individual tracks Indian? (5)

blocks.note: a cur is a contemptible man
RY = railway, the tracks

annotation.surface: A rogue following the trail of a Native American.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Indian' looks like a person; in Britain 'going for an Indian' means an Indian meal, and the question mark marks the stretch.
annotation.definitionFit: In British speech 'an Indian' can mean an Indian meal, such as a curry.

entries.clue: Wine finally quaffed by Pacific Northwest people — afraid of claret? (9)

indicators.note: finally means at the end, so only the word's last letter is used
drunk by, so taken inside

blocks.note: the Squamish, First Nations people of British Columbia, drinking the E
last letter of wine

annotation.surface: Pacific Northwest drinkers finishing off the wine yet somehow nervous of red.
annotation.walkthrough: Claret is red wine, which suits the drinking surface, but it is also old slang for blood.
annotation.definitionFit: Squeamish people faint at the sight of blood, and claret is slang for blood.

entries.clue: Boxers in communication after fracture get niggly (5,5)

indicators.note: communication here is talk between people, so the word counts as it is spoken, not spelt
this piece follows the fracture

blocks.note: a fracture is a split
hares famously box each other in spring

annotation.surface: Boxers exchanging words after a broken bone and getting tetchy.
annotation.walkthrough: Boxers are not fighters but hares, which rear up and box in the mating season.
annotation.definitionFit: An idiom: quibbling over tiny distinctions is the fussy, carping behaviour 'get niggly' describes.

entries.clue: Bar in EastEnders? (4)

blocks.note: not a pub counter but a cake of something you wash with
a long-running BBC television serial; the question mark says it is one example of a kind

annotation.surface: A pub in the East End of London.
annotation.walkthrough: EastEnders is a BBC television soap opera set in London's East End, and its pub, the Queen Vic, makes 'bar' feel like part of it.
annotation.definitionFit: A bar is a cake of soap, and EastEnders is an example of a soap opera.

entries.clue: Educational classic and hot novel (10)

indicators.note: new, so the letters are put in a new order

blocks.note: anagram fodder, 10 letters

annotation.surface: A blurb for a school reading list: a classic plus a hot new novel.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Novel' sits where a book should be but is an adjective meaning new, telling you to rearrange.
annotation.definitionFit: Scholastic means to do with schools and education.

entries.clue: Country region of Spain ablaze to the west (7)

indicators.note: a part of the following words
in an across clue, westward means right to left

blocks.note: sp(AIN ABLA)ze, read backwards

annotation.surface: News of a Spanish region on fire in the west.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface asks for a Spanish region such as Galicia; the region is only a stretch of the letters.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain category definition: the answer is one particular country, in the Balkans.

entries.clue: Price to pay, a toll for still water (9)

blocks.note: the bill is the price to pay
taken as it stands
a bell's toll goes bong

annotation.surface: A road toll charged for still water, as if bottled.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Toll' reads as a road charge beside 'price to pay'; it is the sound of a bell. 'Still water' looks like the bottled kind.
annotation.definitionFit: A billabong is an Australian backwater pool, water that does not flow.

entries.clue: Bugs Bunny ate carrots originally with green-looking one (7)

indicators.note: originally means at the origin, so each word gives only its starting letter
the next pieces are added on

blocks.note: first letters of Bunny, ate, carrots
looking green = looking sick
I = one, the Roman numeral

annotation.surface: Bugs Bunny munching carrots next to a sickly friend.
annotation.walkthrough: Bugs Bunny is a single cartoon name, but 'Bugs' is the definition and 'Bunny' starts the wordplay.
annotation.definitionFit: Bacilli are rod-shaped bacteria, bugs in the germ sense.

entries.clue: Ready, a cover when pulled back opens up (7)

indicators.note: drawn backwards, so the letters run in reverse

blocks.note: ready = set, as in 'ready, steady, go'
taken as it stands
a lid is a cover; all three pieces are then read backwards

annotation.surface: Something ready to open once its cover is pulled back.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface makes 'pulled back' sound like peeling off a cover, which is just what the letters do.
annotation.definitionFit: To dilate is to widen or open up, as a pupil does.

entries.clue: Put up with bagged cat hissing initially (7)

indicators.note: put in a bag: the cat goes inside SAC
initially means at the start, so only the word's first letter is used

blocks.note: a sac is a bag, and the cat is put in it
a tom is a male cat
first letter of hissing

annotation.surface: Putting up with a cat that hisses when it is stuffed into a bag.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Bagged' does double duty: it says the cat goes in, and the bag it goes in is a SAC.
annotation.definitionFit: A figurative verb: what you can keep down in your belly, you can tolerate.

entries.clue: Tender-hearted cabal affiliated to a party (7)

indicators.note: attached to, so placed after

blocks.note: taken as it stands
a do is a party
a ring is a secret group, a cabal

annotation.surface: A political clique that has attached itself to a party, yet is soft-hearted.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Party' reads as political beside 'cabal' and 'affiliated'; it is a do, a social event.
annotation.definitionFit: Adoring means full of love, fond and tender.

entries.clue: American gull seen round northern European port (7)

indicators.note: placed around the next letter

blocks.note: A = American
a gull is a dupe, a fool; A TWERP goes round N
N = northern

annotation.surface: A seagull from America spotted circling a northern European harbour.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Gull' is the seabird in the surface, but here it is a gullible person, a twerp.
annotation.definitionFit: A category definition: the answer is one of Europe's busiest harbours, on the Scheldt in Belgium.

entries.clue: You couldn’t see me for dust in Asian country (4)

blocks.note: the opening of the idiom; it gives no letters but frames the boast of running away
the speaker, me, turned into the subject of a sentence
'you couldn't see me for dust' is said of someone who fled fast, kicking up dust

annotation.surface: A boast of a quick getaway, leaving a cloud of dust across an Asian country.
annotation.walkthrough: The whole phrase is one idea: 'you couldn't see me for dust' means I ran away very fast.
annotation.definitionFit: A category definition: the answer is one particular state in western Asia.

entries.clue: Fleshy tissue in fat apostle wobbling about (4,6)

indicators.note: shaking, so the letters are jumbled

blocks.note: anagram fodder, 10 letters

annotation.surface: A portly apostle whose flesh wobbles as he moves.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface pictures a wobbling belly; the tissue is in the mouth.
annotation.definitionFit: The soft palate is the fleshy back part of the roof of the mouth.

entries.clue: Stop wearing a uniform, I’m taking leave! (5)

indicators.note: put on, so the stop word sits inside A and U

blocks.note: taken as it stands
an engine that stops dies
U = uniform in the phonetic alphabet

annotation.surface: A soldier announcing he is stepping out of uniform and going on leave.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Taking leave' sounds like military leave; it means saying goodbye.
annotation.definitionFit: Adieu is a farewell, what you say as you take your leave.

entries.clue: Score, after losing opener and tail end, completely collapsed (4)

indicators.text: losing opener and tail end, completely
indicators.note: both the first and the last letter are removed

blocks.note: a score is twenty; its first letter and its last both go

annotation.surface: A cricket side losing its opening bat and its tail and folding completely.
annotation.walkthrough: The cricket words are the trick: the opener and tail end are the first and last letters of twenty. In cricket the tail is the weak lower batting order.
annotation.definitionFit: 'Went' can mean gave way or collapsed, as in 'the roof went'.

entries.clue: Old girlfriend I fancy — pardon? (9)

blocks.note: an ex is a former partner
I is one as a Roman numeral
to rate someone is to think highly of them, fancy them

annotation.surface: Someone admitting they still fancy their ex, then asking 'pardon?' as if mishearing.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Pardon?' looks like a request to repeat; it is the verb for clearing someone.
annotation.definitionFit: A near synonym: clearing someone of blame frees them as a pardon does.

entries.clue: Some lemon? That would be a surprise (5)

blocks.note: a curl of lemon peel dropped into a cocktail
an unexpected turn in a story's plot

annotation.surface: Someone astonished to be offered a bit of lemon.
annotation.walkthrough: The question mark admits the first definition is loose: a twist is only one form some lemon takes.
annotation.definitionFit: A twist is a curl of citrus peel, and an unexpected turn in a story.

entries.clue: Succeed as photojournalist — capiche? (3,3,7)

blocks.note: a photojournalist succeeds by getting the picture
capiche = do you understand?

annotation.surface: A photographer being asked whether they understand the job.
annotation.walkthrough: Capiche is slang from Italian for 'understand?', and 'get the picture?' asks the same.
annotation.definitionFit: A photojournalist's job is to get the picture, and 'get the picture?' means 'understand?'.
